problem: Imitation-learned visual navigation policies depend on scarce, costly real-world expert demonstrations with limited action diversity, so they learn geometric obstacle avoidance poorly and are conservative. Cross-embodiment foundation models are also not tailored to a specific robot's capabilities.
motivation: In most robotics settings data is scarce, unlike in autonomous driving. Classical geometric planners with privileged elevation maps can cheaply produce diverse, embodiment-specific, safe trajectories, and the paper argues that data diversity matters more than raw quantity.
key_idea: Augment ~6h of teleoperated legged-robot demonstrations with thousands of hours of MPPI-planner trajectories to randomly sampled goals (using elevation-map traversability), and train a small transformer policy that maps a single RGB image plus an SE(2) goal to an SE(2) waypoint path.
insight: Geometric supervision from a planner adds goal and action diversity that teleop data lacks. On the diverse Daug test set, SPL rises from 49.7 (teleop-only) to 80.0 (augmented), while performance on teleop-style goals is preserved. Training on just 5 augmented missions matches training on 41 teleop-only missions, so diversity rather than sheer quantity drives generalization. A 32M-parameter embodiment-specific model also outperforms the open-loop 7B OmniVLA on goal reaching.
method: Policy architecture: frozen DINOv2 ViT-S/14 (LayerNorm tuned) patch embeddings plus learned positional embeddings; the SE(2) goal is projected and replicated N=50 times as waypoint queries; a 4-block transformer decoder cross-attends to the patches; a shared linear head outputs N SE(2) waypoints (~32M params, 10M trainable).

MPPI planner: samples velocity sequences (vx, vy, ω) under a piecewise-constant SE(2) dynamics model. Cost = traversability (CNN on elevation map) + geodesic goal distance (plus heading near goal) + effort; N=50, dt=0.1s.

Teleop dataset Dtel: fixed-horizon (5s) goal-conditioned segments from recorded GrandTour trajectories, with the goal set to a future pose and time-warping when the goal is within the horizon; stationary segments filtered out.

Geometric dataset Dgeo: for every frame, K=10 goals are sampled from a Gaussian in the robot frame (mean 5m ahead) and labeled with MPPI paths using elevation maps. Infeasible goals still yield safe exploratory or best-effort paths. Dgeo has 1.29M training samples (~1792h) and Daug = Dtel ∪ Dgeo (~1949h).
Training: L2 regression on waypoints, AdamW with OneCycleLR, 16 epochs, batch 16 on one RTX 4090.

Multi-camera variant: shared DINOv2 encoder on front, left and right cameras with a per-view positional embedding, used for real-robot closed-loop runs to avoid forgetting obstacles that leave the front FOV.
Real deployment: runs at 6 Hz on a Jetson Orin on an ANYmal D with a lookahead path follower.

setting.backbone: DINOv2 ViT-S/14 (frozen except LayerNorm) + 4-block transformer decoder, trained from the pretrained encoder
setting.training_data: GrandTour (ANYmal D, 6h, 49 sites): Dtel 113k samples (~157h) plus MPPI-labeled Dgeo 1.29M samples (~1792h); Daug 1.40M samples train
setting.observation: single front RGB image (multi-camera front+left+right variant for real robot)
setting.action_space: predicted SE(2) waypoints (50 waypoints over 5s) tracked by a lookahead path follower
setting.simulator: none; offline evaluation on held-out real GrandTour missions with elevation-map-based collision/geodesic metrics, plus real robot
setting.privileged: Elevation maps / traversability used only for training-time planner labels and for evaluation metrics; none at inference

numbers_note: Custom offline benchmark on held-out GrandTour missions, not a standard navigation benchmark. Ablation results (fewer geometric paths, fewer missions) are only in figures. Real-robot results are qualitative.
results: On the diverse Daug test set, the augmented LiMo reaches SPL 80.0 / SR 82.2 versus 49.7 / 51.4 for teleop-only training, and beats open-loop OmniVLA (SPL 33.5) and straight-line paths (SPL 76.9). On teleop-style goals it is roughly on par with the teleop-only model (86.4 vs 84.4 SPL). The planner oracle with privileged maps reaches 95.4 SPL. The policy runs at 6 Hz on-robot in obstacle-course, dynamic-obstacle and corridor demos.
limitations: Planner labels depend on elevation/traversability estimates that can fail (e.g., cliff edges judged safe), and visual diversity remains bounded by the 6h base dataset.
Single-frame policy without memory forgets obstacles outside the FOV, so real-robot runs needed side cameras; failures on glass, nets and snow.
Evaluation is limited: a custom offline benchmark with planner-reachable goals, an open-loop OmniVLA comparison, and no on-robot baseline comparisons or quantitative real-robot metrics.
